To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dual task costs increase with age in both memory encoding and walking performance.
the effect size of dual-task costs increased with advancing age in both memory and walking tasks.
the dual task of walking and memorizing word lists became increasingly difficult with age, and that the effect size of this increase was greater in the domain of memory than walking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how cognitive control is affected by the demands of concurrent tasks, especially in old age, and with the role of cognitive control in the regulation of sensory and motor processes.
the question how cognitive and motor functions interact and how they change with age.
the effects of age and task demands on the dual task of walking and memorizing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of age is not on the attentional resources per se but on the efficiency in allocating these resources to the task at hand, which is reflected by the increase in dual-task interference.
the age-related increase in dual-task cost is not due to a decline in cognitive control, as is commonly assumed.
the dual task of memorization while walking becomes more difficult with increasing age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

age-related declines in memory performance and in walking performance are not due to the loss of specific skills or abilities, but rather reflect a loss of the ability to control the use of those skills or abilities.

age-related declines in memory performance are not simply due to a lack of attentional resources, but are rather due to the fact that attentional control is required for the performance of many everyday behaviors, including those involving balance and gait.
aging is associated with increased cognitive load in everyday life, which is reflected in the increased difficulty of performing multiple tasks simultaneously.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dual-task costs in the cognitive and motor domains are increased with age, and that these costs may be a useful measure of the functional impact of age-related changes in the brain.
dual-task performance is more difficult in older adults than young and middle-aged adults.
the aging brain is not as efficient at allocating attentional resources as the young brain.
